edition.deck: Brazil and Serbia see major election shifts as Israel votes; in the UK, the Budget looms amid storms, court cases and rising concern over cocaine-related abuse.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises consequential developments and fresh reporting. Budget coverage is framed as reported expectations ahead of Wednesday’s announcement; allegations and unresolved results are attributed rather than presented as settled fact.

content.headline: Lula’s comeback reshapes Brazil’s politics, with digital campaigning in focus
content.shortHeadline: Lula’s comeback puts Brazil’s digital campaigning in focus
content.standfirst: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva overturned a first-round deficit to win re-election, defeating Flávio Bolsonaro. His supporters credit a huge WhatsApp campaign with helping turn the race around, though its direct effect on votes is unknown.

image.caption: Lula and Geraldo Alckmin address supporters after winning the runoff in São Paulo.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Democracy always’: Lula vows no return to dictatorship in Brazil after election win
Brazil election 2026: Full second round results as Lula wins comeback against Flávio Bolsonaro
How 'Lula's Army' WhatsApp chat helped turn Brazil election around

segments.body: Lula won 51.79% of the runoff vote to Bolsonaro’s 48.21%, a margin of more than four million votes, after trailing in the first round. In São Paulo, he told supporters: “Democracy always, dictatorship never again.” Bolsonaro rejected the result; leaders across the political spectrum recognised Lula’s victory.

segments.title: A campaign fought online and on the ground
segments.body: A WhatsApp channel called Lula’s Army grew to 10.8 million followers between the two rounds, urging supporters to share campaign material and recruit voters. Allies credit it with boosting Lula’s comeback, but political scientists say its direct effect cannot be measured and point to grassroots campaigning and efforts to persuade undecided voters as part of the result.

content.headline: Israel votes in close election as Hebron operation displaces thousands
content.shortHeadline: Israel votes as Hebron operation displaces thousands
content.standfirst: A close contest is putting Benjamin Netanyahu’s security record and Israel’s political direction under scrutiny. In Hebron, nearly 2,000 Palestinians have been displaced during an Israeli military operation ahead of election day.

image.caption: A screen in Tel Aviv shows Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot ahead of the election.

sources.originalTitle: What you need to know about the most consequential election in Israel’s history
Deeply divided Israel braces for pivotal election
‘It’s collective punishment’: nearly 2,000 Palestinians in Hebron displaced as Israeli forces take over homes

segments.body: Israelis vote on Tuesday in the first general election since the 7 October 2023 attacks. Polls suggest Netanyahu’s coalition may lose its majority, but opposition parties are divided and may struggle to form a government. The campaign has focused on security, the state of Israel’s democratic institutions and the future of ultra-Orthodox military exemptions.

segments.title: Displacement in Hebron
segments.body: In Hebron, the municipality says 370 families—nearly 2,000 people—have been displaced during a military sweep following a gun attack that killed two Israeli soldiers. Residents told the Guardian they were forced from their homes; the Israeli army said civilians who wished to leave were permitted to do so temporarily. The city remained sealed off to cars, according to the report.

content.headline: Serbia’s Vučić concedes defeat to student-backed election movement
content.shortHeadline: Vučić concedes defeat to Serbia’s student-backed movement
content.standfirst: Aleksandar Vučić says his party has lost a snap parliamentary election after a student-led anti-corruption movement surged to victory. The final count is not complete, and the movement now faces the challenge of turning its campaign into government.

image.caption: Celebrations in Serbia after Aleksandar Vučić conceded defeat.

sources.originalTitle: Celebrations in Serbia after veteran ruler Vučić loses election to student-led protest movement
Serbian leader Aleksandar Vučić ousted by student movement in seismic election
How a movement of students brought down Serbia's Vučić

segments.body: With 97% of polling stations counted, Serbia’s election commission said the Student List had won 2.25 million votes and Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party 1.67 million. Vučić conceded, saying: “It is clear we have lost these elections.” Preliminary figures cited by the BBC put the Student List on 52.7% and the SNS on 39.2%; the final result remains outstanding.

segments.title: From protest to parliament
segments.body: The movement grew out of protests after 16 people died when a canopy collapsed at Novi Sad station in 2024. It fielded candidates from across society rather than putting students on the ballot. Its representatives will now have to organise a parliamentary majority and deliver on anti-corruption promises, while the movement itself has no obvious leader.

content.headline: UK sanctions Sudanese commanders over alleged sexual violence at El Fasher
content.shortHeadline: UK sanctions Sudanese commanders over alleged sexual violence
content.standfirst: Britain has imposed travel bans and asset freezes on 15 commanders from Sudan’s warring forces, citing suspected sexual violence during the siege and fall of El Fasher. Tens of thousands of civilians were killed or remain unaccounted for, according to the report.

image.caption: RSF defectors arrive to surrender to the Sudanese military in Omdurman.

sources.originalTitle: UK sanctions Sudanese military leaders implicated in El Fasher ‘campaign of rape’

segments.body: The UK sanctioned 15 commanders from the Rapid Support Forces and Sudanese Armed Forces on the first anniversary of El Fasher’s fall. The Foreign Office said the action was intended to ensure the horrors there were known. The sanctions target individuals suspected of sexual violence; they are not findings of guilt.

segments.title: A city emptied by war
segments.body: Up to 10,000 people are believed to have been killed over two days when the RSF took the city after an 18-month siege, and another 40,000 remain unaccounted for. Fewer than 70,000 people are believed to remain in El Fasher, compared with a pre-war population of more than one million. Sudan’s conflict has forced 14 million people from their homes, the report says.

content.headline: US airstrikes in Somalia raise fears of civilians trapped by floods
content.shortHeadline: Somalia airstrikes raise fears civilians could be trapped by floods
content.standfirst: Residents and analysts allege that US-led strikes are pushing people in al-Shabaab-held areas towards the flood-prone Juba River as El Niño threatens severe flooding. US Africa Command denies targeting civilians or using weather as a weapon.

image.caption: A US special operations colonel with a Somali soldier in Mogadishu in 2023.

sources.originalTitle: US forces accused of ‘weaponising’ Somalia’s floods by trapping women and children in the path of El Niño

segments.body: Residents in and around Jilib told the Guardian that frequent airstrikes have made movement difficult and driven people towards the Juba River. A source monitoring the floodplain said the offensive appeared to be exploiting the risk of flooding. The report says residents described civilian deaths, but US Africa Command declined to give operational details and denied using floods to displace people.

segments.title: Flood risk and limited help
segments.body: The Juba basin is a particular concern for UN agencies, and the International Committee of the Red Cross expects severe flooding. Local officials warn that a lack of boats could leave thousands stranded; they say aid funding has fallen sharply and flood preparations remain inadequate. The report does not establish that the US has deliberately used weather as a military tactic.

content.headline: China’s party meeting follows sweeping purges of senior officials
content.shortHeadline: China’s party meeting follows sweeping leadership purges
content.standfirst: A closed-door Communist Party meeting could give Xi Jinping a chance to tighten discipline and shape priorities ahead of next year’s Party Congress. The scale of recent military purges has left senior ranks unusually depleted.

image.caption: The Fifth Plenum is a closed-door meeting of China’s Communist Party leadership.

sources.originalTitle: China's big political meeting could see Xi 'tighten discipline' in party

segments.body: The four-day Fifth Plenum brings together about 300 members of the Communist Party’s Central Committee. A Politburo readout says it will address “comprehensive strict governance” of the Party, a phrase interpreted as signalling tighter discipline. The meeting’s conclusions are expected to be published after it ends on Thursday.

segments.title: Purges leave gaps
segments.body: The gathering follows investigations and removals among senior party and military figures. The Asia Society Policy Institute estimates that only two of 44 military members appointed to the Central Committee in 2022 have not been taken down. The Central Military Commission, which runs the armed forces, has been reduced to Xi and one other general, the BBC reports.

content.headline: Anthropic’s planned US listing exposes AI boom’s financial risks
content.shortHeadline: Anthropic’s planned listing puts AI’s financial risks in focus
content.standfirst: The Claude maker has publicly filed for a US stock-market listing, reporting $16.3bn in revenue for the first half of 2026 and an $80bn loss. Its prospectus also sets out risks from AI misuse, dependence on suppliers and regulation.

image.caption: Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei in Bengaluru, India.

sources.originalTitle: Anthropic filing for US stock market listing reveals rapid revenue gains and even larger losses
Anthropic warns of 'catastrophic risk' to humankind ahead of blockbuster share listing

segments.body: Anthropic’s filing offers a first public view of the finances behind one of the biggest prospective technology listings. Revenue rose from $4.6bn in 2025 to $16.3bn in the first six months of 2026, while the company reported a net loss of $80bn for that period. The listing’s timing, share price and size have not been disclosed.

segments.title: Risks alongside growth
segments.body: The company’s prospectus lists potential harms from misuse of AI, loss of control, authoritarian abuse and economic disruption. It also warns of reliance on a small number of customers and outside computing providers. Anthropic has separately said advanced AI could pose catastrophic or existential risks if deployed without appropriate safeguards.

content.headline: Ebola response worker killed as Uganda tightens border rules
content.shortHeadline: Nurse killed responding to Ebola alert as Uganda tightens border
content.standfirst: A nurse was killed and another health worker injured while responding to an Ebola alert in north-eastern DR Congo. Uganda has restricted non-essential travel across its border and says returning citizens will face 21 days in quarantine.

image.caption: A health worker in DR Congo, where an Ebola response nurse was killed.

sources.originalTitle: Nurse killed in attack while responding to Ebola alert in DR Congo

segments.body: The workers were attacked by local youths who accused them of contaminating water and spreading Ebola, according to UN-backed Radio Okapi. The World Health Organization condemned the attack and said health workers must be able to work safely. The BBC says it has contacted the Ebola response team for details about the circumstances.

segments.title: Cross-border concerns
segments.body: Uganda has barred non-essential travel to and from DR Congo and says returning Ugandans will be quarantined for 21 days. Health authorities are investigating cases linked to travel through Uganda; they say no cases have been reported within the country since August. The current outbreak has caused nearly 10,000 infections and more than 4,800 deaths in DR Congo, according to the report.

content.headline: Budget expected to boost defence while science centres face funding cuts
content.shortHeadline: Budget expected to boost defence as science centres face cuts
content.standfirst: Ahead of Wednesday’s Budget, reports point to billions in extra defence investment and possible cuts to science facilities including Jodrell Bank. The government has not confirmed the full proposals, which would expose competing demands on public money.

image.caption: Jodrell Bank in Cheshire, whose future funding is in question.

sources.originalTitle: UK’s Budget message to Trump – as Healey to borrow billions for defence boost
Who could be badly hit by the Budget – and the people who might end up better off
The iconic site Burnham vowed to save – that allies warn is at risk from his Budget

segments.body: Chancellor John Healey is expected to use borrowing and state investment funds to support defence companies, while addressing a reported £4.7bn shortfall in the Defence Investment Plan. The i Paper reports that a £15bn rise in defence spending over four years is planned, but that the government may delay a decision on its 3% of GDP target until next year’s spending review.

segments.title: Science funding under pressure
segments.body: Scientists, union representatives and regional leaders have urged the Chancellor to protect research facilities, including Jodrell Bank, which is not currently prioritised for further funding after March 2028. They say cuts could damage UK research and local economies; the government points to a record £86bn investment in research and development. The Budget is expected to clarify whether any sites will be protected.

content.headline: Burnham says Brexit weakened the economy and border control
content.shortHeadline: Burnham says Brexit weakened the economy and border control
content.standfirst: The prime minister says the UK’s Brexit settlement has not delivered as promised, but rules out major changes in this parliament. His comments reopen a divisive debate over closer EU ties and what the government might seek at next month’s summit.

image.caption: Andy Burnham speaks in the House of Commons.

sources.originalTitle: Brexit deal is not good enough for British public, says Andy Burnham
Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement

segments.body: Andy Burnham said Britain had ended up with a harder Brexit than voters were offered in the referendum, weakening the economy and the UK’s ability to control immigration. He said he would like to see the UK rejoin the EU in his lifetime, but would not move ahead of public opinion or propose rejoining during this parliament.

segments.title: Political disagreement over the next step
segments.body: Burnham says the government wants practical steps to improve relations with the EU, including cooperation on immigration at a summit on 20 November. Conservatives and Reform UK oppose a return to free movement; the Liberal Democrats argue closer ties could help growth. Labour MPs in some Leave-voting constituencies are concerned that reopening the debate could benefit Reform UK.

content.headline: Two storms kill two people as 90,000 UK properties remain without power
content.shortHeadline: Two storms kill two as 90,000 UK properties remain without power
content.standfirst: Storms Austen and Boelo brought deaths, flooding and widespread disruption over the weekend. Power companies say about 90,000 customers were still without electricity on Monday, with further strong winds forecast for parts of the UK.

image.caption: Waves crash over a lighthouse at Newhaven harbour during Storm Austen.

sources.originalTitle: About 90,000 properties still without power after two storms strike Britain

segments.body: Two men died after being struck by falling trees in Scotland and north London. Power operators restored service to about 700,000 customers over the weekend, but roughly 90,000 remained without power on Monday morning. The Energy Networks Association said continuing high winds had made repairs difficult and dangerous.

segments.title: More wind on the way
segments.body: The Met Office issued two yellow warnings for strong winds: one covering western coastal areas from Cornwall to south-west Scotland, and another covering much of Scotland on Tuesday. Forecasters warned of possible travel cancellations, road closures and further power cuts. Flooding and transport disruption were also reported over the weekend.

content.headline: Chris Brown gets suspended sentence for London nightclub bottle attack
content.shortHeadline: Chris Brown gets suspended sentence over nightclub bottle attack
content.standfirst: The R&B singer received an eight-month prison sentence, suspended for 12 months, after pleading guilty to affray over an attack in a London nightclub. The judge called the violence serious and dangerous; Brown will not be jailed unless he commits another offence during the suspension period.

image.caption: Chris Brown leaves court after sentencing.

sources.originalTitle: Chris Brown given suspended eight-month prison sentence over nightclub attack
Sangeren Chris Brown får otte måneders betinget fængsel i voldssag

segments.body: Brown was sentenced at Southwark Crown Court for hitting music producer Abraham Diaw with a glass bottle in a Mayfair nightclub in 2023. The court heard the attack lasted about 20 seconds and that Diaw needed hospital treatment. Brown and his vocal coach, Omololu Akinlolu, both pleaded guilty to affray; Akinlolu received a suspended four-month sentence.

segments.title: Judge calls attack dangerous
segments.body: The judge said the repeated blows to the head with a bottle were “plainly dangerous” and that Brown’s fame did not entitle him to special treatment. More serious charges, which Brown denied, were dropped. The sentence was suspended under changes to sentencing law; the judge said immediate imprisonment was not justified in the circumstances.

content.headline: Russell Brand’s former assistant tells trial his behaviour was normalised
content.shortHeadline: Former assistant tells court Brand’s behaviour was normalised
content.standfirst: A former assistant told Southwark Crown Court she was asked to obtain female fans’ phone numbers and became “sick of him”. Brand denies rape, sexual assault and indecent assault charges brought by six women; the trial continues.

image.caption: Russell Brand arrives at Southwark Crown Court.

sources.originalTitle: Russell Brand had ‘insane sexual appetite’ and his bad behaviour was normalised, trial told
Russell Brand asked assistant for female fan phone numbers, court hears

segments.body: Helen Berger, who worked for Brand from 2006 to 2007, told the court that he asked her to get phone numbers from female fans. She said the request made her uncomfortable and that she eventually told him she would not do it. Her statement described a workplace where she felt those around him had normalised his behaviour.

segments.title: Charges denied
segments.body: Brand faces three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault relating to six women and allegations spanning 1999 to 2009. He denies the charges. His defence says sexual activity was consensual and that accounts have been affected by a 2023 television documentary. The prosecution is due to finish on Tuesday morning.

content.headline: Visa and Mastercard face potential £5bn UK group claim over fees
content.shortHeadline: Visa and Mastercard face potential £5bn claim over UK fees
content.standfirst: Law firms have applied to pursue a group claim alleging the card companies overcharged UK businesses through interchange fees. Mastercard disputes the case; it could take years to conclude and businesses may be included unless they opt out.

image.caption: Visa and Mastercard are defending the fees at the centre of a proposed claim.

sources.originalTitle: Visa and Mastercard threatened with potential £5bn UK lawsuit over fees

segments.body: Harcus Parker and Hausfeld have applied to the Competition Appeal Tribunal to bring a claim over fees paid by businesses through their banks when customers use Visa or Mastercard. The firms estimate the claim could be worth about £5bn, including interest, for fees charged since October 2020. The tribunal has not yet approved the application.

segments.title: Who could be included
segments.body: If the application succeeds, about one million UK businesses, organisations and charities with revenues below £100m could be included automatically unless they opt out. Larger businesses would need to opt in. Mastercard called the claim speculative and defended interchange fees as supporting the payments system; Visa said it believes the fees benefit consumers, merchants and banks.

content.headline: Cocaine detected in nearly six in 10 tested domestic abuse suspects
content.shortHeadline: Cocaine detected in nearly six in 10 tested abuse suspects
content.standfirst: Home Office figures show cocaine in nearly six in 10 police drug tests of people arrested on suspicion of domestic abuse. The figures cover those tested, not all suspects, and do not establish that cocaine caused the alleged abuse.

image.caption: Cocaine use is examined in a report on domestic abuse.

sources.originalTitle: ‘He was like 10 men after taking cocaine‘: how Britain’s drug habit is fuelling domestic abuse

segments.body: The Home Office figures, supplied to the Guardian, cover police drug tests from July 2025 to June this year. The report notes that some tests were conducted because officers already suspected drug use, so the results cannot show how common cocaine use is among all domestic abuse suspects. A previous pilot study found a similar share tested positive for cocaine or opiates.

segments.title: Survivor and support workers describe risks
segments.body: Charlotte, who says her former partner’s cocaine use intensified his paranoia and violence, described repeated assaults and said she has been free of alcohol and cocaine since leaving him. A domestic abuse therapist said cocaine may worsen existing controlling behaviour, but does not make someone abusive if they were not already. Support workers are calling for more research.

content.headline: UK youth jobs review considers Dutch model of paid internships
content.shortHeadline: UK youth jobs review considers Dutch-style paid internships
content.standfirst: A government review of young people not in work or education is expected to consider longer college courses and paid work placements, drawing on the Netherlands. The review is due next month; no recommendations have yet been adopted.

image.caption: An apprentice welds at a Dutch vocational training programme.

sources.originalTitle: The new plan for five-month paid internships to get young people off benefits

segments.body: Alan Milburn’s review is expected to examine a Dutch vocational course that includes two paid 20-week placements and more teaching hours than are typical in UK colleges. The Netherlands has a 4.9% rate of young people aged 18 to 24 not in work, education or training, compared with 15.1% in the UK, according to the report.

segments.title: Questions about implementation
segments.body: The Association of Colleges says longer placements could give young people work experience and confidence, but UK employers have been reluctant to commit to long placements. An employment and learning providers’ group also argues that foundation apprenticeships should be shorter. The government declined to comment; Milburn’s report has not yet been published.

content.headline: Southern Denmark region sends contested LGBTQ+ handbook back for rewrite
content.shortHeadline: Southern Denmark region orders rewrite of LGBTQ+ handbook
content.standfirst: A majority on the Region of Southern Denmark council voted for a new draft of guidance for healthcare staff working with LGBTQ+ people. The debate exposed a sharp political divide over gender language and how the guidance should address patients.

image.caption: Mette With Hagensen speaks during the regional council’s debate on the handbook.

sources.originalTitle: 'Jeg skal lige sluge det menneskesyn': Håndbog sendt tilbage efter hård debat

segments.body: The regional council voted to send the handbook back for a new draft after a conservative majority supported an amendment. The guidance is intended to help healthcare staff when they meet LGBTQ+ patients, including examples of gender-neutral pronouns. The first draft had already been rejected by a majority in the regional executive committee.

segments.title: Divided views on the guidance
segments.body: Venstre’s Pernelle Jensen argued that the handbook imposed terminology on staff and disputed its wording about gender. Social Democrat Mette With Hagensen opposed changing it, saying healthcare should make room for difference and meet people’s needs. A contributor to the handbook asked what scientific or medical basis informed the claim that there are only two genders; the council chair cited biology books and teaching.

content.headline: Danish-Swedish man charged after Swedish police find 31 weapons
content.shortHeadline: Danish-Swedish man charged after Swedish police find 31 weapons
content.standfirst: A Danish-Swedish man faces charges of aggravated weapons possession after police found 31 firearms, more than 14,000 rounds of ammunition and Nazi memorabilia in Sweden. He denies being a Nazi; police say there is no charge alleging a planned attack.

sources.originalTitle: I svensk skov fandt politiet våbenlager, Hitler-buste og SS-mærker. Og det hele tilhørte en dansker

segments.body: Police found the weapons and ammunition at a home and a storage building in Gullringen, Sweden, according to a case file obtained by DR. The man is also charged over possession of a small quantity of drugs and flammable or explosive materials. The prosecutor has called it one of Sweden’s largest weapons seizures, according to the report.

segments.title: No charge of a planned attack
segments.body: The man is not charged with planning an attack. Investigators found extremist messages in his chats, including calls for the death of Jews; he told police this was joking jargon and said the Nazi objects were part of a collecting interest. He said the weapons came from a late uncle. The case is due in court in Kalmar in November.

content.headline: Holmegaard glassworks cuts planned redundancies to 50
content.shortHeadline: Holmegaard glassworks halves planned redundancies to 50
content.standfirst: Ardagh Glass Holmegaard near Næstved says negotiations and voluntary departures have reduced planned dismissals from 100 to 50. The factory is closing a furnace and two production lines, while 98 roles will be removed overall.

image.caption: Ardagh Glass Holmegaard is carrying out a round of job cuts near Næstved.

sources.originalTitle: Efter forhandlinger bliver fyringsrunde på sydsjællandsk glasværk halveret

segments.body: The glassworks says 50 employees will be dismissed after negotiations reduced the number from an initial plan of 100. The company will also have 27 voluntary departures, will not renew some temporary contracts and will leave vacant posts unfilled. In total, 98 positions are being removed.

segments.title: Factory cuts production
segments.body: Ardagh says it is closing a furnace and two production lines to avoid the risk of the entire business shutting. Managing director Kim Holmberg said staff would be told on Monday and Tuesday whether they would keep their jobs. The company recorded a DKK20m loss in the spring after six months of an emballageafgift it had opposed, the report says.

content.headline: Man arrested in Køge on suspicion of selling illegal medicines
content.shortHeadline: Man arrested in Køge over suspected illegal medicine sales
content.standfirst: A 33-year-old man is suspected of selling illegal medicines through social media and a website, Denmark’s National Special Crime Unit says. Police found a quantity of counterfeit medicine at his home; his response to the allegation is not known.

sources.originalTitle: 33-årig anholdt i aktion mod ulovlig medicin

segments.body: The National Special Crime Unit said it arrested the man on Monday and found a larger quantity of counterfeit medicine at his address. The investigation began after the Danish Customs Agency intercepted a package addressed to him containing 4,000 pieces of packaging for prescription medicines.

content.headline: New Danish outlet Y plans to use AI across news production
content.shortHeadline: New Danish outlet Y plans AI-led news production
content.standfirst: The free outlet Y launches on Tuesday with ambitions to use AI in much of its reporting and distribution. Its editor says journalists will remain responsible for the work; a media researcher says its value will depend on producing original journalism and earning readers’ trust.

image.caption: Michael Dyrby leads the new Danish news outlet Y, which plans to use AI in much of its production.

sources.originalTitle: I morgen går nyt AI-medie i luften: 'Vi går faktisk mod strømmen'

segments.body: Y says AI will help with everything from developing story ideas and selecting sources to production and distribution, while editors will conduct interviews and remain accountable for published work. The outlet plans to start with text and audio versions and eventually produce 40 to 50 articles a day. It launches at 13:00 on Tuesday.

segments.title: Originality and trust in question
segments.body: Roskilde University media researcher Aske Kammer says the key test is how much original reporting Y produces, rather than repackaging work from other outlets. He sees potential in making stories available in different formats, but is sceptical about whether the business can be sustainable while readers remain wary of AI-generated content.

content.headline: Danish house prices widen the gap between Skive and Copenhagen
content.shortHeadline: House prices widen the gap between Skive and Copenhagen
content.standfirst: Since 2013, prices have risen 75% nationally and more than 150% in Copenhagen, while Skive prices are up just 9%—below general inflation. Researchers disagree on whether that divergence is a problem, as jobs and population increasingly concentrate in larger centres.

image.caption: A graphic showing how Danish house prices have risen at different rates across the country.

sources.originalTitle: Professor om skævt boligmarked: Hvis det skal løses, skal stavnsbåndet genindføres

segments.body: Boligsiden figures show house prices in Skive have risen by 9% since 2013, compared with 75% nationally and more than 150% in Copenhagen. An economist at the Danish Housing Economics Centre says the divide can affect household equity and later spending, while a Copenhagen Business School lecturer argues lower prices also make housing more affordable in Skive.

segments.title: Jobs and population follow growth
segments.body: A VIVE researcher says people, businesses and jobs have increasingly concentrated in central Denmark over the past 15 years, while outlying areas lose residents and employment. A Skive family said they could buy a house there for DKK1.4m after finding that their budget in Aalborg would only stretch to a two-room flat. Researchers say there is no quick fix; improved public transport could help towns near larger job markets.

content.headline: Dónal Lunny, a defining figure in Irish music, dies aged 79
content.shortHeadline: Irish music great Dónal Lunny dies aged 79
content.standfirst: The multi-instrumentalist and producer helped shape groups including Planxty, the Bothy Band and Moving Hearts, and was widely credited with bringing the bouzouki into Irish music.

image.caption: Dónal Lunny performing at the Manchester Apollo in 1999.

sources.originalTitle: Dónal Lunny, ‘colossus of Irish music’, dies aged 79

segments.body: Dónal Lunny, the Irish traditional musician and producer, has died aged 79 from cancer. A founding member of Planxty, he also played with the Bothy Band, Moving Hearts and Coolfin, and produced 17 albums through his label, Mulligan Records.

segments.title: A lasting musical legacy
segments.body: Ireland’s president, Catherine Connolly, called Lunny central to many of the most influential moments in Irish music over six decades. She highlighted his partnerships with Christy Moore and Andy Irvine, his work as a producer and the recognition he received from fellow artists, including a lifetime achievement award at the 2025 RTÉ Radio 1 Irish Folk Awards.

content.headline: Jimmy Webb revisits the songs he wrote for Dolly Parton, Glen Campbell and Frank
content.shortHeadline: Jimmy Webb brings his lost songs back to life
content.standfirst: The 80-year-old songwriter discusses a new album of previously unheard material, the performers who made his classics endure and the friendships and losses behind his long career.

image.caption: Jimmy Webb in 1971.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I don’t give a damn what people think any more!’ Jimmy Webb on his wild days – and writing hits for Dolly, Glen and Frank

segments.body: Jimmy Webb’s songs, including “Wichita Lineman”, “By the Time I Get to Phoenix” and “MacArthur Park”, have continued to find new audiences. He says Nick Cave and Flea have recorded “Wichita Lineman”, while the song’s reach has also been renewed through recent performances and recordings by other artists.

segments.title: Songs left in the drawer
segments.body: Webb’s new album, “Yours for the Taking: The Found Songs of Jimmy Webb”, gathers previously unheard songs, including material first intended for Dolly Parton and Frank Sinatra. He recalls Sinatra gently telling him that “Winter Clothes” was not quite finished; Webb says he finally returned to it years later.

content.headline: Sam Fender says high ticket prices for his stadium tour will be changed
content.shortHeadline: Sam Fender promises changes to stadium ticket prices
content.standfirst: After fans highlighted standing tickets listed at more than £130 for his 2027 tour, Fender said he was unhappy with the prices and promised the tiered standing arrangement would not go ahead.

image.caption: Sam Fender, who said he was unhappy with the tour’s ticket prices.

sources.originalTitle: Sam Fender tells fans high ticket prices for Proper Massive tour are ‘getting changed’

segments.body: Sam Fender has promised to change ticket prices for his 2027 stadium tour after fans criticised the cost of tickets advertised for Wembley. Standing tickets were listed at £98.85 and £130.75, with seats ranging from £64.75 to £130.75.

Fender said the prices had risen more than he intended and that they should reflect the cost of putting on the show. He also called the division between front and back standing areas “bollocks”, saying it would not happen on his tour. Tickets were due to go on sale on Friday, with a presale on Wednesday.

content.headline: James Dean Bradfield reflects on Manic Street Preachers’ ‘The Holy Bible’
content.shortHeadline: Manic Street Preachers face the weight of ‘The Holy Bible’
content.standfirst: The band’s new live release revisits the album whose lyrics were shaped by Richey Edwards. Bradfield describes the strain of performing it, the group’s response to Edwards’ disappearance and the limits of closure.

image.caption: Manic Street Preachers: Nicky Wire, James Dean Bradfield and Sean Moore.

sources.originalTitle: Manic Street Preachers: ‘We just weren’t equipped to deal with Richey’s problems’

segments.body: Manic Street Preachers have released “The Holy Bible Live”, recorded during a 2014 performance of their 1994 album in full. Frontman James Dean Bradfield recalls the anniversary concerts as a physical and emotional challenge: some lyrics, he says, weighed heavily on stage, while the band wanted to perform as a three-piece to evoke the group’s former line-up.

segments.title: Living with an absence
segments.body: Lyricist Richey Edwards disappeared in 1995 and is presumed to have died by suicide. Looking back on his bandmate’s mental health struggles, Bradfield says they were young and “just weren’t equipped to deal with it”, even though they tried to help. He rejects the idea that grief necessarily brings closure, while saying he is proud the band managed to connect with the album again.

content.headline: A Taylor Swift fan remembers discovering her on Myspace in 2006
content.shortHeadline: Before Taylor Swift was famous, fans found her on Myspace
content.standfirst: On the 20th anniversary of Swift’s debut album, a former teenage fan recalls the online community that formed around her early songs—and how an outsider’s discovery became a global phenomenon.

image.caption: Taylor Swift as a teenage country singer.

sources.originalTitle: The Taylor Swift I knew on Myspace in 2006

segments.body: Before Taylor Swift became a global star, the writer and a friend found her music through Myspace, where Swift shared details of her life and career. The essay recalls how teenagers exchanged comments, collected press clippings and made listening to a new country singer feel like belonging to a private club.

segments.title: A changing relationship with fame
segments.body: Swift’s self-titled debut, released in October 2006, offered songs about teenage relationships that made a strong connection with young listeners. Looking back, the writer sees both the closeness of Swift’s early online presence and the distance created by her subsequent fame, while reflecting on the way she helped make female songwriting and fan participation more visible.

content.headline: Heavensouls turns digital overload into intimate, shifting sound on ‘cantu of th
content.shortHeadline: Heavensouls makes a restless collage feel intimate
content.standfirst: On “cantu of the sower”, producer Chidi Obialo combines free-jazz movement, electronic fragments and live instrumentation in a restless collage that the review hears as both disorienting and emotionally searching.

sources.originalTitle: cantu of the sower EP

segments.body: The 20-year-old producer heavensouls, also known as Chidi Obialo, builds “cantu of the sower” from shifting layers of percussion, strings, saxophone, samples and small electronic sounds. The review describes the album-length EP as a “collage of collages”, with pieces that move between apparent chaos and moments of calm.

The review connects the music’s density to Obialo’s movement between Nigeria, the US and online musical communities, while noting his stated interest in the claustrophobia of suburban life. Its sounds can feel crowded, but the critic finds that the record’s collisions are shaped by a personal thread rather than overload for its own sake.

content.headline: Caroline Rose finds humour and unease in ‘Gentling the Horse at the Walt Whitman
content.shortHeadline: Caroline Rose’s new album makes room for oddballs
content.standfirst: The singer-songwriter’s seventh album turns a long-delayed song into a noisy, funny set of portraits, with suburban unease and more sombre reflections beneath its restless surface.

sources.originalTitle: Gentling the Horse at the Walt Whitman Mall

segments.body: Caroline Rose’s “Gentling the Horse at the Walt Whitman Mall” brings the long-gestating “Yip Yip Yow” to the front of an album of distorted guitars, fast tempos and comic characters. The review hears a deliberate break from the melancholy of Rose’s previous record, while finding that the jokes often carry darker concerns.

Rose’s songs look at outsiders and people struggling at the edges of everyday life. The reviewer points to “Conversation with Shiv”, which revisits a friend caught in drug use and financial trouble, as evidence that the album’s humour and its more vulnerable moments coexist rather than cancel each other out.

content.headline: Amy Winehouse’s ‘Back to Black’ reissue adds demos but leaves its legacy intact
content.shortHeadline: ‘Back to Black’ reissue adds detail, not a new story
content.standfirst: The 20th-anniversary edition includes a handful of unheard recordings, demos and a live set. The review celebrates Winehouse’s album while arguing that the extra material cannot fill the gap left by her lost work.

sources.originalTitle: Back to Black (20th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: Amy Winehouse’s “Back to Black” remains the centrepiece of a 20th-anniversary set that adds early versions of songs, B-sides and a live recording from Amsterdam. The review finds the demos illuminating, particularly for showing how the album’s sound developed, and again praises Winehouse’s voice and the record’s mix of vintage influences with contemporary songwriting.

segments.title: What an archive cannot restore
segments.body: The new material is limited, and the review notes that the recordings Winehouse made for a planned follow-up were destroyed. The set offers useful glimpses into her work, but the critic argues that no anniversary package can replace the music that was never released.

content.headline: ‘Animol’ director Ashley Walters on prison, sobriety and breaking a cycle
content.shortHeadline: Ashley Walters turns hard-won experience into ‘Animol’
content.standfirst: After a career shaped by music, prison and acclaimed acting roles, Walters has directed his first feature. He discusses sobriety, masculinity and the memories that informed its young-offender setting.

image.caption: Ashley Walters, director of “Animol”.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Nothing worked for me until I was clean and sober’: Ashley Walters on acting, directing – and turning his life around

segments.body: Ashley Walters has directed “Animol”, a drama set in a young offenders’ institution. He says the film is not autobiographical, but drew on memories of his own time in prison. Its story follows teenagers navigating fear and violence, while also making room for tenderness and a queer romantic relationship.

segments.title: A different idea of masculinity
segments.body: Walters reflects on his own struggles with addiction and says he has been sober since entering rehabilitation in 2020. He sees a connection between “Animol” and “Adolescence” in their attention to young people and to the ways restrictive ideas about masculinity discourage men from talking about vulnerability.

content.headline: ‘All About the Money’ finds a wealthy heir and a commune’s unresolved tensions
content.shortHeadline: A commune, an heir and a film that leaves questions open
content.standfirst: Sinéad O’Shea’s documentary follows James “Fergie” Chambers, a multimillionaire who bankrolled a rural Massachusetts commune. The review finds a vivid, complicated subject, but says the film’s attempt at balance leaves its story unsettled.

image.caption: James “Fergie” Chambers in “All About the Money”.

sources.originalTitle: All About the Money review – confusion and compelling weirdness of wealthy leftwing heir

segments.body: James “Fergie” Chambers, an heir to a multimillion-dollar fortune, helped fund a small communist community in rural Massachusetts. After some members were arrested following a protest at an Israeli-owned arms manufacturer, the documentary follows the fallout among Chambers and former members, including Paige Belanger, while Chambers is abroad.

segments.title: An uneasy portrait
segments.body: The review praises filmmaker Sinéad O’Shea’s effort not to take sides, but says the result can feel muddled and leaves basic questions about the subject and the commune unresolved. Chambers is also facing a US extradition request from Spain over alleged support for Hamas; the review presents him as a compelling, troubled figure without resolving the allegations.

content.headline: Ashley Walters, Cyndi Lauper and more on why ‘That Thing You Do!’ endures
content.shortHeadline: Why “That Thing You Do!” still feels like a feelgood film
content.standfirst: A writer revisits Tom Hanks’s 1996 music comedy, finding joy in its fictional band’s sudden success and warmth in its refusal to pretend that creative lives always end happily.

image.caption: The fictional band the Wonders in “That Thing You Do!”.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Vicarious wish-fulfillment’: why That Thing You Do! is my feelgood movie

segments.body: Tom Hanks wrote, directed and starred in “That Thing You Do!”, the story of a fictional 1960s pop group whose fortunes change when a new drummer speeds up its song. The essayist recalls the thrill of the band hearing its music on the radio, and the film’s affection for the excitement of making something together.

segments.title: Hope without a perfect ending
segments.body: The film’s success is short-lived: relationships and competing ambitions pull the band apart. For the writer, that wistfulness is part of its appeal. The story offers the pleasure of vicarious success without hiding the trade-offs, and ultimately suggests choosing happiness over fame.

content.headline: ‘Never After Dark’ review: a Japanese ghost story with old-school charm
content.shortHeadline: A ghostbuster meets her match in “Never After Dark”
content.standfirst: Moeka Hoshi plays a travelling exorcist hired to investigate a haunting in Dave Boyle’s Japanese-language horror film, which the review finds charming and inventive even when its scares are familiar.

image.caption: Moeka Hoshi in “Never After Dark”.

sources.originalTitle: Never After Dark review – ghostbuster-for-hire meets her match in Japanese exorcism horror

segments.body: In “Never After Dark”, Moeka Hoshi plays Airi, a travelling ghostbuster whose dead sister appears to her in mirrors. A new job at a former hotel brings her into contact with a spirit whose damaged face hints at a more difficult haunting than she expected.

The review praises the film’s physical effects and its inventive use of reflections, wire work and a phenakistoscope in the exorcism scenes. It finds the scares somewhat predictable, but says Hoshi brings intelligence and spontaneity to a film that is otherwise a low-stakes, playful horror story.

content.headline: ‘Ever Since I Knew Myself’ examines childhood and conformity in Georgia
content.shortHeadline: A filmmaker revisits childhood and Georgia’s classrooms
content.standfirst: Maka Gogaladze’s debut documentary pairs conversations with her mother with observations of children’s lessons, examining strict education and the pressure to conform in Georgia.

image.caption: A classroom scene in “Ever Since I Knew Myself”.

sources.originalTitle: Ever Since I Knew Myself review – confronting the scars of childhood

segments.body: Maka Gogaladze opens her debut feature by recalling how, as an adolescent, she threw away her poems in an act of rebellion against her mother. She later puts her mother on camera to discuss demanding piano lessons and examinations that continued to trouble her into adulthood.

segments.title: Beyond one family
segments.body: The film also observes children in history, ballet, dance and art classes, where the review sees an emphasis on discipline and little room for individual expression. It says the shifts between personal memories and these wider scenes can feel abrupt, but points to the film’s interest in how national identity and collectivism shape education.

content.headline: ‘The Social Reckoning’ turns Facebook’s harms into a personal warning
content.shortHeadline: “The Social Reckoning” looks at Facebook’s impact—and ours
content.standfirst: Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up to “The Social Network” dramatises reporting on Facebook’s internal research. The writer found it frightening, but questions how readily viewers can separate their own lives from the company’s influence.

image.caption: Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in “The Social Reckoning”.

sources.originalTitle: I was terrified watching The Social Reckoning – then went back to scrolling

segments.body: “The Social Reckoning” centres on Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz and former Facebook employee Frances Haugen, whose disclosures exposed internal research into the platform’s effects, including its impact on teenage girls and the promotion of extremist groups. Jeremy Strong plays Mark Zuckerberg in the film, written and directed by Aaron Sorkin.

segments.title: The harder question
segments.body: The review describes the film as a tense investigation that makes social media’s influence feel close to home. But its writer returns to scrolling after watching, acknowledging a dependence on Meta’s services for work and social connection. The film’s warning, the essay argues, matters in part because many people feel unable simply to leave.

content.headline: Why women are falling for the basket-made husband in “Wicker”
content.shortHeadline: The unlikely appeal of “Wicker”’s basket-made husband
content.standfirst: The film’s unusual romance—about a woman who commissions a basketmaker to weave her a husband—has sparked online fascination. Its creators and commentators connect the appeal to domestic labour, desire and outsiderhood.

sources.originalTitle: A husband made from a basket? Why women are going wild for freaky film romance Wicker

segments.body: In “Wicker”, Olivia Colman plays a fisherwoman who asks a basketmaker, played by Peter Dinklage, to make her a husband. Alexander Skarsgård plays the resulting wicker man. The trailer and a suggestive promotional popcorn bucket helped prompt a wave of online jokes and fan enthusiasm.

segments.title: A fantasy with a domestic edge
segments.body: Filmmakers Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson say the character’s attentiveness is part of the appeal: he notices work that needs doing without expecting praise. Writer Gillian Daniels and academic Indira Neill Hoch place the film among monster romances that explore desire, difference and what audiences consider attractive or threatening.

content.headline: Elizabeth Holmes remains a mystery in the documentary ‘You Can See Everything’
content.shortHeadline: A new documentary returns to Elizabeth Holmes’s story
content.standfirst: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim follow Holmes before she reports to prison, letting her defend herself without resolving the central question: whether her claims of innocence reflect conviction or manipulation.

image.caption: Elizabeth Holmes, the subject of “You Can See Everything”.

sources.originalTitle: 'As famous and defiant as ever': Why Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes remains the US's most fascinating fraudster

segments.body: “You Can See Everything” follows Elizabeth Holmes, the convicted Theranos founder, in the period before she reported to prison. In interviews and observed scenes with her family, Holmes insists that she did not lie and that her company’s blood-testing device worked, claims set against her conviction for defrauding investors.

segments.title: Questions without a verdict
segments.body: The film’s directors, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, do not settle how to interpret Holmes. A later conversation adds a voice that questions both her account and Fielder’s response to it. The feature says the documentary’s mix of comedy and unease leaves viewers with competing possibilities rather than a definitive conclusion.

content.headline: “This City Is Ours” returns with its Liverpool gangland drama intact
content.shortHeadline: “This City Is Ours” returns to Liverpool’s criminal world
content.standfirst: The second series brings back the Phelan crime family and its complicated loyalties. The review praises the performances and tension, as well as the small domestic details that keep the drama grounded.

image.caption: James Nelson-Joyce as Michael in “This City Is Ours”.

sources.originalTitle: This City Is Ours review – the Liverpudlian gang drama is back … and the acting’s as terrific as ever

segments.body: The second series of “This City Is Ours” opens with Michael trying to leave the Phelan crime family behind, only to be drawn into a new crisis involving the family of a rival cartel boss. The review praises the ensemble, including Shaun Evans as newcomer Ozzie Thompson, and singles out a tense car-wash sequence.

The series’ appeal, the review argues, lies partly in its unglamorous details: characters worry about IVF, family obligations and everyday chores alongside murder and drug deals. These mundane touches make the drama’s misguided, often violent characters feel more human—and more compelling—than slicker crime-series archetypes.

content.headline: Bill Murray’s Irish golf travelogue struggles to find its way
content.shortHeadline: Bill Murray’s Irish golf show looks like a trip gone wrong
content.standfirst: The review of “A Course Called Ireland” finds strained encounters, awkward narration and long, silent car journeys, with only occasional glimpses of Murray’s charm or reflections on his Irish heritage.

image.caption: Bill Murray in “A Course Called Ireland”.

sources.originalTitle: A Course Called Ireland review – why did Bill Murray ever agree to this Irish golf show?

segments.body: In “A Course Called Ireland”, Bill Murray travels around Ireland playing golf and reflecting on his family history. The review describes a series that appears unsure whether it is about golf, Murray or the Irish, and criticises its decision to use a local woman, Margaret, as an inexperienced narrator.

Murray is often reluctant to follow the production’s prompts, the review says, leaving quiet car journeys and strained conversations that the show tries to cover with forced quirkiness. There are brief moments when he is thoughtful about his Irish ancestry or charming with locals, but they do not rescue the travelogue for the critic.

content.headline: Seven shows to stream this week, from “Nocturne” to Matthew Perry’s story
content.shortHeadline: Seven shows to stream, including a Matthew Perry documentary
content.standfirst: This week’s recommendations range from a prison-set thriller starring Stephen Graham to an intimate series about Matthew Perry, alongside a low-key comedy and a darts contest.

image.caption: Stephen Graham in the thriller “Nocturne”.

sources.originalTitle: Nocturne to The One About Matthew Perry: the seven best shows to stream this week

segments.body: The Guardian’s weekly guide picks seven programmes to stream. Among them is “Nocturne”, a claustrophobic thriller in which Stephen Graham plays a serial killer in a prison psychiatric ward, and a three-part documentary about Matthew Perry, combining interviews with friends and family with an account of his rise and struggles.

The selection also includes “Minimum Wage”, a mockumentary about teenagers running a struggling pizzeria, and a Netflix darts competition featuring amateurs facing champion Luke Littler. The guide describes the latter as a short-format contest where an upset could bring a share of a £501,000 prize.

content.headline: “Escaping Idi Amin” brings Asian Ugandans’ expulsion into view
content.shortHeadline: Ugandan Asians recall Idi Amin’s expulsion order
content.standfirst: A two-part documentary hears from people who were children when Idi Amin ordered Uganda’s Asian population to leave in 90 days, recording memories of violence, fear and displacement.

image.caption: A military officer in “Escaping Idi Amin”.

sources.originalTitle: TV tonight: Idi Amin’s forced expulsion of Asians from Uganda

segments.body: In 1972, Idi Amin gave Uganda’s Asian population 90 days to leave the country. “Escaping Idi Amin” hears from people who experienced the expulsion as children, including accounts of curfews, daily radio countdowns, street violence and massacres.

The programme is a two-part documentary, with the first episode scheduled for BBC Two. The television guide describes its testimonies as complex as well as frightening, bringing personal recollections of the expulsion to the centre of the history.

content.headline: “One Born Every Minute” returns with an intimate account of childbirth
content.shortHeadline: “One Born Every Minute” returns to the delivery room
content.standfirst: The reviewer welcomes the birth series’ return after eight years, arguing that its close attention to three women’s experiences makes visible a major life event often left out of public conversation.

image.caption: Faye with her first baby in “One Born Every Minute”.

sources.originalTitle: One Born Every Minute is back – and it’s wild, essential TV

segments.body: Channel 4’s “One Born Every Minute” returns after an eight-year break, following three women through very different births: a first baby after previous miscarriages, a planned caesarean after a traumatic birth and a later pregnancy. The reviewer, drawing on her own experience of childbirth, calls the episode tense and life-affirming.

segments.title: Making private experience visible
segments.body: The essay argues that birth is often treated as too intimate to discuss, despite its physical and emotional intensity. By showing the women’s experiences and the roles of their partners and medical staff, the programme offers a shared public space for stories that might otherwise be quickly set aside.

content.headline: “Gone Fishing” gives Ted one last trip with Bob Mortimer and Paul Whitehouse
content.shortHeadline: “Gone Fishing” says goodbye to its beloved dog Ted
content.standfirst: The series’ new opener includes a final, posthumous fishing trip for Ted, the much-loved dog who became an unofficial third member of the cast. The review reflects on the show’s warmth and its candid approach to ageing.

image.caption: Ted, the much-loved dog from “Gone Fishing”.

sources.originalTitle: Goodbye Ted, the grumpy canine heart of Gone Fishing

segments.body: A special episode of “Mortimer and Whitehouse: Gone Fishing” brings Ted back for one final trip on the River Ribble. The Patterdale terrier, adopted by executive producer Lisa Clark, died in April. The review recalls how his grumbling persona and comic moments made him a much-loved presence in the series.

segments.title: A show about friendship and time
segments.body: The review notes that the programme has always paired humour with frank conversations about health and ageing. Ted’s absence makes that perspective more poignant, but the writer says the show’s appreciation of nature, friendship and the present keeps the tribute from becoming simply sad.

content.headline: Prince William’s “Graham Norton” appearance was a carefully judged PR move
content.shortHeadline: What Prince William gained from the “Graham Norton” sofa
content.standfirst: The writer sees the prince’s relaxed, full-hour appearance as an effective demonstration of approachability, linking it to Kensington Palace’s effort to shape his public image.

image.caption: Prince William on “The Graham Norton Show”.

sources.originalTitle: The real reason Prince William appeared on Graham Norton

segments.body: Prince William appeared on “The Graham Norton Show” alongside Cate Blanchett, Hannah Waddingham and Robert Irwin, promoting his Earthshot Prize. The essay says he stayed for the full programme, joked with the host and spoke about his interests, creating a more relaxed impression than a brief promotional appearance would have done.

segments.title: A public image at work
segments.body: The writer argues that the appearance fitted an effort to present William as an “average millennial dad” and a forward-looking figure. Comparing it with Prince Harry’s more personal interview, the essay sees the contrast as favourable to William, while acknowledging that the monarchy’s publicity operation is part of the picture.

content.headline: Miranda Hart’s exit from “The Celebrity Traitors” becomes a moment of joy
content.shortHeadline: Miranda Hart brought warmth to “The Celebrity Traitors”
content.standfirst: An essay celebrates Hart’s humour and vulnerability on the reality series, noting that her return to television after years of illness made her exit especially affecting.

image.caption: Miranda Hart in “The Celebrity Traitors”.

sources.originalTitle: Miranda has brought wholesome joy back to TV

segments.body: After seven episodes, Miranda Hart was murdered in “The Celebrity Traitors”. The essay recalls her comic highlights, from the accidental moustache in a challenge to teaching a dance move that inspired the imaginary group “Big Mix”, and says her warmth made her a standout presence.

segments.title: Laughter and connection
segments.body: Hart has spoken about struggling with chronic fatigue syndrome and being largely bed-bound for years. After her exit, she described how meaningful it had been to reconnect with laughter, work and other people. The essay argues that her willingness to show vulnerability helped make the moment moving amid the show’s games and backstabbing.

content.headline: Lara Croft’s 30-year career has had its share of missteps
content.shortHeadline: Lara Croft at 30: the low points as well as the icons
content.standfirst: A look back at “Tomb Raider” highlights the rushed sequels, awkward spin-offs and marketing choices that often misunderstood Lara Croft—even as she remained one of gaming’s defining characters.

image.caption: Lara Croft in “Tomb Raider IV–VI Remastered”.

sources.originalTitle: Lara Croft is 30! We look at the video game icon’s biggest blunders

segments.body: Thirty years after Lara Croft’s debut, the retrospective recalls how “Tomb Raider” became a hit and made its heroine a gaming icon. It also revisits the series’ less successful moments, including annualised releases that wore down developer Core Design and the poorly received “Tomb Raider: Chronicles”.

segments.title: An icon repeatedly misread
segments.body: The article criticises later games and marketing for leaning on Lara’s sexualised image or placing her in stories that diminished her agency. Its broader case is that her lasting appeal comes from being a capable, enigmatic adventurer—and that developers and marketers repeatedly missed what players valued about her.

content.headline: “Penguin Colony” turns an Antarctic expedition into an unsettling adventure
content.shortHeadline: A penguin explores “Penguin Colony”’s strange Antarctica
content.standfirst: This unusual exploration game sends players waddling through an Antarctic landscape shaped by Nazis, Lovecraftian horrors and fragments of language. Its rough edges do not diminish its ambition, the review argues.

image.caption: A penguin in “Penguin Colony”.

sources.originalTitle: Penguin Colony review – an Antarctic odyssey of Nazis and Lovecraftian horrors

segments.body: In “Penguin Colony”, players explore Antarctica as a penguin, moving between ice fields, ruins and increasingly strange landscapes. The game draws on H P Lovecraft’s “At the Mountains of Madness”, but reframes the expedition’s human arrogance through a small bird collecting words rather than treasure.

segments.title: A world built from contradictions
segments.body: The review praises the game’s unsettling combination of low-poly exploration, historical material and a narrator’s account of an earlier expedition. It notes occasional audio and control problems, but says the ending challenges both Lovecraft’s racism and Nazi brutality, and invites players to explore without human-style urgency.

content.headline: Ubisoft Paris moves from Mario to tactical combat with “Rainbow Six Tactics”
content.shortHeadline: How Ubisoft Paris changed gears for “Rainbow Six Tactics”
content.standfirst: The studio behind “Mario + Rabbids” is making a turn-based “Rainbow Six” spin-off. Its developers explain how planning, player choice and realistic settings shape the shift.

image.caption: A scene from “Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics”.

sources.originalTitle: From Mario to machine guns: how Ubisoft Paris made Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics

segments.body: Ubisoft Paris is moving from “Mario + Rabbids” to “Rainbow Six Tactics”, a turn-based spin-off of “Rainbow Six Siege”. The preview describes a mission in Nigeria in which a squad uses drones, explosives and coordinated movement to enter a guarded warehouse.

segments.title: Planning and player choice
segments.body: Creative director Elie Benhamou says the series’ emphasis on preparation and consequential decisions suits a tactics game. He wants players to experiment rather than follow one prescribed route, while level designer Julien Vial describes the challenge of making locations feel realistic compared with the studio’s more fantastical Mario environments.

content.headline: A father and son replay the first game they played together
content.shortHeadline: Replaying “Modern Warfare 2” brings a father and son together
content.standfirst: A father revisits co-op missions from his son’s childhood, finding that better teamwork—and the time they share—matters more than finally completing the game.

image.caption: A scene from “Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2”.

sources.originalTitle: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears

segments.body: The writer and his 22-year-old son return to “Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2”, the first game they played together when the son was five. Older now, they try again at co-op missions they never completed, including one known to them as “the guard dogs in the snow”.

segments.title: More than a high score
segments.body: Their different play styles initially get them into trouble, but they learn to divide the work and communicate. The writer sees the sessions as a rare chance to play without everyday pressures, and as a meaningful period of closeness before father and son move to different parts of the world.

content.headline: New footage renews scrutiny of infant monkey experiments at US lab
content.shortHeadline: Footage renews scrutiny of infant monkey research
content.standfirst: Video released by Peta shows infant macaques in experiments at the University of Washington that ended in 2020. The university says the work contributed to public-health research; the footage has reopened questions about animal welfare and the value of the findings.

image.caption: A still from footage released by Peta showing infant macaque research at the University of Washington.

sources.originalTitle: Peta releases video showing experiments on infant monkeys at University of Washington

segments.body: Footage released by animal-rights group Peta shows newborn macaques separated from their mothers and undergoing neurological tests at the University of Washington’s National Primate Research Center. The experiments, which ran from 2014 to 2020, investigated possible effects of prenatal exposure to domoic acid, a toxin produced by marine algae.

segments.title: What the research established
segments.body: Records cited in the report say researchers administered domoic acid to 32 pregnant macaques and removed 28 infants from their mothers after birth. The university says the studies contributed to understanding how prenatal exposure may affect learning and memory. The report says there is no clear evidence the work changed public-health recommendations.

segments.title: Welfare questions remain
segments.body: Peta and primate-welfare experts criticise separating the infants from their mothers. The university says maternal relationships and early development are important welfare considerations and that experienced staff cared for the animals. It says there are no current infant studies at the centre, though protocols for such studies remain active.

content.headline: Phone photos help researchers track changing shorelines across 21 countries
content.shortHeadline: Phone photos track changing shorelines
content.standfirst: CoastSnap turns repeat photographs taken by the public into a record of beach change. Researchers use the images to study erosion, storm impacts and whether beach replenishment schemes are working.

image.caption: Praa Sands beach in Cornwall, where a CoastSnap station helps researchers monitor shoreline change.

sources.originalTitle: How citizen science is tracking changes in shorelines around the world

segments.body: CoastSnap invites people to place a phone in a fixed cradle at a beach and send in a photograph. Because the camera position stays roughly the same, software can align images taken over time, map the shoreline and adjust for the tide using each photo’s timestamp.

Researchers use the resulting records to follow longer-term coastal erosion, examine the effects of individual storms and monitor beach replenishment. The project, which began in Australia in 2017, now has more than 200 stations in 21 countries and is described as the largest coordinated land-based coastal monitoring programme in the world.

content.headline: Data centre boom pits local communities against AI infrastructure plans
content.shortHeadline: The data centre boom meets local resistance
content.standfirst: Residents are challenging the noise, land use and potential pollution of new data centres, while companies warn that opposition could delay construction. The debate is over who benefits from the infrastructure—and who bears its costs.

image.caption: Protesters oppose a data centre in North Ayrshire.

sources.originalTitle: The datacentre next door: on the frontline of tech’s latest David v Goliath battle
Big, noisy and coming to a town near you - why the data centre backlash is growing
Data centers could erase decades of air quality gains
AI firms say UK has a year to head off datacentre protests before construction is threatened

segments.body: The rapid expansion of data centres built to support cloud services and AI is bringing conflict to communities near proposed and operating sites. In Newport, residents describe losing light and facing persistent noise from a growing campus; in Cardiff, a proposed facility on a hospital park-and-ride site has drawn more than 1,200 planning objections. The BBC counts about 12,250 data centres worldwide, up from roughly 8,000 operational sites in 2021.

segments.title: Power has an environmental cost
segments.body: A Houston Advanced Research Center analysis modelled possible pollution from Texas data centres over five years. If all planned projects draw from the anticipated grid mix, it estimates power-sector soot could more than triple and nitrogen oxide emissions rise 136% from 2025 levels. The outcomes depend on how much proposed capacity is built and how it is powered: onsite renewables could reduce nitrogen oxides, while gas engines could worsen pollution.

segments.title: Industry seeks public consent
segments.body: A taskforce including Nvidia, Microsoft and Cisco says the UK has about a year to establish a community-benefit “compact” before opposition threatens projects. It proposes letting host councils keep more tax revenue. The UK government says data centres should bring jobs and investment, prioritise clean power and use water responsibly.

perspectives.body: Campaigners dispute that local benefits can be secured by financial incentives alone. PauseAI UK warns communities may see such offers as being bought off; Action to Protect Rural Scotland says organised opposition is already growing.

content.headline: AI-assisted search uncovers serious flaws in widely used PHP software
content.shortHeadline: AI finds long-hidden flaws in PHP
content.standfirst: Researchers used AI tools to identify vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language used across much of the web. No successful attacks had been reported in the gathered coverage, but organisations worldwide took systems offline or rushed to patch them.

sources.originalTitle: What is PHP and why did it spark a global cyber-security scramble?
Race to update services' computer systems after cyber-security flaw found
'It's been relentless' say IT workers on frontline of PHP cyber-security scramble

segments.body: Researchers using tools developed by OpenAI helped uncover two serious vulnerabilities in PHP, a back-end programming language used by websites including Wikipedia, online shops and WordPress sites. Cybersecurity firm Wiz estimates PHP powers 70% of the world’s websites. The PHP Foundation rated the flaws 9.2 out of 10 in severity; under the right conditions, attackers could take control of affected servers.

segments.title: The response—and what remains unknown
segments.body: Governments and businesses took some sites offline as a precaution while patches were prepared and applied. The PHP Foundation urged users to update immediately. The coverage reported no successful attacks at the time, but researchers warned that further attempts were likely and that the full impact could take months to emerge. Website operators need to update PHP itself; updating WordPress or its plugins alone does not fix the flaw.

segments.title: A scramble for IT teams
segments.body: Administrators described long hours rebuilding or updating systems, including older applications that no longer receive support. They also warned that rumours about active exploits and inaccurate security alerts added to the pressure. One cybersecurity researcher cautioned that poorly calibrated warnings could lead to “alert fatigue” when a genuinely exploitable flaw emerges.

perspectives.body: The BBC’s interviews with IT workers show the human cost of the response: administrators had to balance precautionary shutdowns against rapid fixes, while trying to distinguish reliable guidance from unverified reports.

content.headline: Microsoft offers voluntary buyouts to as many as 60,000 employees
content.shortHeadline: Microsoft offers buyouts to up to 60,000 staff
content.standfirst: The voluntary exit offer covers selected teams in the US, UK, Canada and India. Microsoft says it is a new approach to workforce change; reporting points to wider cost-cutting and efforts to reshape staffing around AI.

sources.originalTitle: Microsoft offers buyouts to 60,000 employees
Microsoft offers buyouts to around 60,000 employees, reports say

segments.body: Microsoft is offering voluntary buyouts to as many as 60,000 employees across the US, UK, Canada and India, according to reports by The Verge and TechCrunch. The offer applies to selected teams and does not include all parts of the business. Microsoft says it gives eligible staff financial support and career-planning resources if they choose to leave.

The Verge reports that eligibility spans some AI, Copilot, Windows, Xbox and other teams, while some groups are excluded or only partly included. Microsoft says the offer is not based on age, length of service or performance. TechCrunch characterises it as part of the company’s latest efforts to cut costs and rework its workforce for AI; the company did not immediately respond to its request for comment.

content.headline: West Virginia town debates the public-safety promise and privacy risks of Flock
content.shortHeadline: A town weighs surveillance against safety
content.standfirst: Huntington’s debate over automated license-plate cameras exposed sharp disagreement over crime prevention, privacy safeguards and public consent. A contract passed, but the city’s later rules and an effort to challenge the decision leave the dispute unresolved.

sources.originalTitle: The city that fought Flock

segments.body: Huntington’s city council approved a contract for Flock’s automated licence-plate reader system by a 6–4 vote after a lengthy public meeting. Supporters pointed to cases in which the company’s network helped police locate suspects or missing people. Opponents warned that linking vehicle sightings across locations could enable intrusive tracking or misuse by police.

segments.title: Safeguards and opposition
segments.body: The city later approved an ordinance setting permitted and prohibited uses, requiring a list of authorised users, quarterly audits and deletion of data after 30 days. Critics questioned whether the rules adequately protect residents and hold officers accountable. A community group said it had collected 1,600 signatures by mid-September toward the roughly 2,700 needed to trigger a city vote on its proposed ban.

content.headline: Farmers in Northern Ireland use cameras, robots and apps to manage herds
content.shortHeadline: Technology changes how Northern Ireland farms work
content.standfirst: Farmers describe using camera systems to flag possible cattle health problems, robotic milking and apps to organise records. Their experience also highlights how better broadband has enabled digital tools in rural areas.

image.caption: Farmer George McMaster uses technology to help manage his herd near Islandmagee, County Antrim.

sources.originalTitle: From agriculture to AI-griculture: How tech is changing farming

segments.body: On a farm near Islandmagee, County Antrim, an AI camera assigns cows individual IDs and flags changes in their movement that may indicate lameness. Farmer George McMaster says it has identified problems he did not spot by eye. Other farmers interviewed by the BBC use robotic milking machines and apps to manage herd records, inspections and medicines.

Reliable broadband has helped another farmer run an online-connected farm shop and use digital systems for daily work. The tools support farmers’ decisions rather than replacing them, says FarmDrive developer Gareth McDonald. The examples show how digital infrastructure, as well as farm equipment and software, shapes whether rural businesses can use these services.

content.headline: Anthropic’s IPO filing exposes huge losses, AI risks and founder control
content.shortHeadline: Anthropic’s IPO tests the AI boom—and its safeguards
content.standfirst: The Claude maker has filed to list on Nasdaq, reporting rapid revenue growth alongside major losses and extensive risks. Its proposed governance structure would leave founders with substantial voting control even as public investors enter.

sources.originalTitle: Anthropic filing for US stock market listing reveals rapid revenue gains and even larger losses
Anthropic officially files for its public debut
Anthropic’s IPO filing lays out a plan to ‘revolutionize every area of human endeavor’ with AI
Anthropic warns of 'catastrophic risk' to humankind ahead of blockbuster share listing

segments.body: Anthropic plans to list on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, in a public offering that will test investor appetite for AI companies. Its filing reports $16.3bn in revenue for the first half of 2026. TechCrunch says the company recorded a $693m operating loss over that period, while its $80.7bn net loss was largely driven by noncash accounting adjustments tied to convertible debt.

segments.title: Risks, spending and control
segments.body: Anthropic’s filings warn that its models could cause serious harm if misused and that safeguards may fail; the company also describes potential benefits in science, medicine and productivity. The Verge reports large commitments for computing capacity from cloud providers and SpaceX. The proposed listing’s timing, share price and amount to be raised have not been disclosed.

segments.title: Who will hold the votes?
segments.body: TechCrunch reports that seven co-founders would collectively control 50.1% of shareholder voting power through a Founder LLC, while Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust would appoint most of the board. The company says this structure is intended to protect its public-benefit mission; it would give public shareholders limited practical influence.
